title: “the form of the fourth is like the Son of God” — who is the fourth man in the furnace?
summary: In Daniel 3:24–25 the king sees “four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire” when three were cast in, and says “the form of the fourth is like the Son of God”. At 3:28 he blesses the God who “hath sent his angel”. The verses do not say who the fourth is.
text: KJV Daniel 3:24: “Did not we cast three men bound into the midst of the fire?”. KJV Daniel 3:25: “Lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt; and the form of the fourth is like the Son of God”. KJV Daniel 3:28: “Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who hath sent his angel, and delivered his servants”.
reasoning: The king counts three bound and four loose, and describes the fourth by likeness (“like the Son of God”). Later he names an angel as the one God sent. The passage does not say that the fourth is the angel, nor that the fourth is the Son of God; it gives the king’s words at two moments. Possible readings, named only as readings: the fourth is the angel of 3:28; the fourth is a divine figure the king describes in the words he has; the fourth is a figure of a kind the king describes and nothing more is said. The record does not decide between them.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to the verses quoted. The record does not say that any reading is the right one, does not rest on the Aramaic or the Greek (the Greek’s addition between 3:23 and 3:24 is the subject of a separate T record), does not examine other passages that use “Son of God”, and does not claim that no other passage says more.

sides.label: A
sides.quote: the form of the fourth is like the Son of God

title: “Darius the Median took the kingdom” — who is Darius, and how does his reign stand to the reign of Cyrus?
summary: Daniel 5:31 has “Darius the Median” take the kingdom, 9:1 calls him “the son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes”, and 6:28 speaks of “the reign of Darius, and … the reign of Cyrus the Persian”. Daniel 1:21 and 10:1 count years of Cyrus. The verses do not say how the two reigns relate.
text: KJV Daniel 5:31: “And Darius the Median took the kingdom, being about threescore and two years old.” KJV Daniel 9:1: “In the first year of Darius the son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes, which was made king over the realm of the Chaldeans”. KJV Daniel 6:28: “So this Daniel prospered in the reign of Darius, and in the reign of Cyrus the Persian.” KJV Daniel 1:21: “And Daniel continued even unto the first year of king Cyrus.” KJV Daniel 10:1: “In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia”.
reasoning: Darius is given a people (Median or of the seed of the Medes), a father’s name and an age, and 9:1 says he “was made king”, which does not say by whom. Cyrus is given the title “king of Persia” at 10:1 and “the Persian” at 6:28. Chapter 6:28 can be read as two reigns, one after another, or as one person’s reign told under two names or titles with “and” between them. The verses quoted do not say which, and they do not say whether the years of Cyrus in 1:21 and 10:1 count from the same point as the reign of Darius. Possible readings, named only as readings: two successive kings; one person under two names; Darius as a ruler under Cyrus. The record does not decide between them.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to the verses quoted. The record does not say that any reading is the right one, does not rest on the Hebrew, Aramaic or Greek (the Greek name at 11:1 is the subject of a separate T record), does not use outside histories, does not examine the published question about the kings named in Ezra 4, and does not claim that no other passage says more.

sides.label: A
sides.quote: Darius the Median took the kingdom

title: “sent to king Jareb” — who is king Jareb?
summary: Hosea 5:13 has Ephraim go “to the Assyrian” and send “to king Jareb”, and 10:6 has the calf carried “unto Assyria for a present to king Jareb”. The verses do not say who Jareb is.
text: KJV Hosea 5:13: “then went Ephraim to the Assyrian, and sent to king Jareb”. KJV Hosea 10:6: “It shall be also carried unto Assyria for a present to king Jareb”.
reasoning: The name appears twice, each time after a king of Assyria or Assyria itself, with the word “king” before it. It is not said whether Jareb is the Assyrian king under a name, a title, or another king named in parallel with the Assyrian. Possible readings, named only as readings: a name of the king of Assyria; a title or epithet for the king of Assyria; a different king to whom Ephraim sends. The record does not decide between them.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to the two verses quoted. The record does not say that any reading is the right one, does not rest on the Hebrew or the Greek, and does not claim that no other passage says more. A word search of the packaged KJV, whole word and case-sensitive, found the name only at these two verses.
